In educational lectures, presenters often combine text and images to convey information more effectively than through text alone. However, current lecture processing systems mainly focus on slide text. We propose a novel dataset known as LMD, specifically designed for slides with mixed modality to support educational content. The dataset comprises 1,500 lectures from 80 different courses and comprises 15,000 unique slides, along with 90,000 text images. We also introduce a baseline model that can identify key concepts discussed in lectures by combining text and image information. Notably, our model outperforms existing approaches in this area. The dataset and code are publicly available for further research purposes. We believe that LMD has the potential to drive future research on multimodal lecture processing. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/UKPLab/multimodal_lecture_displays. Further information can be found at https://ukpllab.mede.ucl.ac.uk/mld. This significant variation arises from the distinct jet energy corrections used for light and b flavored jets, which may introduce flavor bias into the measurement. To minimize this bias, the collaboration has developed an alternative method for evaluating the top quark mass, utilizing flavor-independent jet energy corrections. Temporal video modeling heavily relies on the gradient flow between frames, 
but current methods of tracking this flow are computationally expensive and time-consuming. 
This paper proposes a novel video modeling approach called Gradient forward-transmission (GF-T) 
that leverages the flow between frames to significantly accelerate the computation. 
The GF-T model consists of two main components: a feature forward-transmission (FFT) block 
and a temporal module that enables efficient large-scale temporal modeling. 
The FFT block uses the flow between frames to quickly compute feature differences, 
while the temporal module aggregates the differences across frames to capture long-term dependencies. 
Experimental results demonstrate that GF-T achieves substantial speedups with minimal accuracy loss. 
The authors also introduce a multi-scale GF-T (MS-GF-T) model that enables more efficient and accurate video modeling.

We present WikiGUM, a large, multi-class dataset aimed at advancing the field of wikification, which involves automatically classifying and categorizing entities found within text. Unlike previous entity linking or classification datasets, which only group entities into broad categories such as location, person, and so on, WikiGUM takes a more detailed approach by grouping them into 12 more specific categories. This finer-grained categorization allows for a more nuanced evaluation of how well an entity linking system performs on different types of entities. To facilitate the development of more accurate entity linking systems, we provide a dataset of 1,200 human-annotated documents with 7,500 entity mentions that have been grouped according to WikiGUM's classification system. To further enhance the evaluation of these systems, we also release a corresponding set of 1,200 entity links that have been generated by state-of-the-art entity linking systems for comparison purposes. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving a mean F1 score of 0.73 on the full dataset and 0.81 on the most general category of entities. Covert channels in 5G, 6G, and beyond enable stealthy data transmission via authorized communication networks, compromising network security.  Covert channel detection in MAC layer broadcast signals is challenging due to their public nature, as established methods are unsuitable for detecting covert data in these signals.  A novel approach is presented to detect covert data in MAC layer broadcast signals by analyzing power features of base station signals.  Base station signal power modulation is used to extract a power sequence, which is then converted into a binary sequence and analyzed using power analysis techniques.  A power analysis method is employed to detect covert data transmission, yielding accurate results in both simulated and real-world scenarios.  A comparative analysis of this method against existing detection approaches is also presented.  Ultimately, this work paves the way for further research on detecting covert channels in 5G, 6G, and future wireless networks. Deep neural networks often produce overly detailed feature maps during the prediction process, leading to inefficient inference and significant computational overhead, particularly in resource-constrained environments. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel training method called In-Training Representation Correlation mitigation (IRC-m) that enables the learning of more compact features. IRC-m achieves this by introducing a secondary loss term that encourages the learning of representations with reduced redundancy. This is achieved by monitoring representation correlations during the training process and penalizing the learning of overlapping representations. As a result, IRC-m leads to the development of more efficient features that can be easily compressed through binarization. To validate the effectiveness of IRC-m, we conduct comprehensive experiments across various computer vision tasks and show that it significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. The research findings open up promising avenues for developing NMT systems that can learn from related text samples.  The research code and evaluation results are publicly available. A novel visual loop closure method is introduced that incorporates a two-way connection establishment between a current frame and all previous frames, as well as to all subsequent frames, in the trajectory covered by a mobile robot. This method is built upon the concept of the RANdom SToNed (RANSAC) algorithm, which is utilized to determine the essential geometric information required for loop closure. Unlike traditional methods that rely on a single direction of closure, our approach enables the robot to establish a loop with any of its preceding or succeeding frames, thus significantly enhancing the robustness of the RANSAC algorithm. In addition, our method is capable of significantly improving the performance of visual SLAM systems, such as those employing ORB-SLAM2, by streamlining the process of loop detection and closure. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in both simulating and real-world environments. The challenge of creating a balanced and efficient spatial map involves two conflicting goals: maintaining stability and accuracy. Stability ensures that small changes in the map data will result in small changes in the map layout, while accuracy involves assigning points to their closest landmarks. However, previous approaches to this problem have been hindered by a fundamental instability issue. In this research, we first formalize the root cause of this instability and then develop a new algorithm to address it. Our approach is based on a key insight that any stable map must satisfy two conditions: it must be a perfect representation of a grid and any two points must be assigned to their closest landmarks in the map. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective algorithm that improves any initial map to meet these conditions. Our experimental results demonstrate that this algorithm produces maps that are both stable and accurate, surpassing the performance of existing methods in terms of speed and quality. Additionally, we investigate the computational complexity of this problem and show that it belongs to a class of difficult computational problems that requires a new approach. Machine learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can significantly degrade their performance. Adversarial techniques, such as fooling a model into misclassifying data, have been extensively researched. However, a lesser-known adversarial approach is the antagonistic assault, which aims to maximize the confidence of a model's incorrect predictions. This paper explores the application of antagonistic assaults to fraudulent activity detection in commercial payment systems. We develop a novel antagonistic assault method tailored to tabular data and test its effectiveness in identifying fraudulent transactions. Our findings show that antagonistic assaults can be used to flag suspicious transactions and outperform standard classification algorithms in this domain. We also demonstrate that antagonistic assaults can be used to create synthetic data samples for imbalanced classes without modifying the underlying model. Our results indicate that this approach can generate additional training data to improve model performance in class imbalance scenarios. Finally, we provide a case study of creating synthetic data using antagonistic assaults to predict customer churn in telecom companies. Our analysis reveals that antagonistic assaults can generate high-quality synthetic data for imbalanced classes and outperform traditional methods in this context. Overall, this research highlights the potential of antagonistic assaults in identifying fraudulent activity and creating synthetic data for imbalanced classes. The coefficient inverse problem for the Riemannian Radiative Transfer Equation involves determining the scattering coefficient using a known solution and boundary data. Research has shown that this problem is highly complex and difficult to solve analytically. This paper aims to develop a novel numerical approach for solving this inverse problem by employing a convexification technique. Our method involves transforming the original nonlinear problem into a linear, convex optimization problem, and it does not rely on the existing Riemannian Pencil Model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using synthetic data and compare its performance with other numerical methods. Our results indicate that this approach is highly efficient and accurate, even with noisy data. Furthermore, we apply our method to real-world problems in geophysics and medicine, including oil reservoirs and lung tumor imaging. Our findings suggest that this method is well-suited for practical applications. Transformers are notoriously memory-hungry, making them difficult to use in low-memory environments. To mitigate this, we've developed a novel approach called Gating Dropout, a flexible regularization technique that works within transformer architectures. By applying Gating Dropout to the feed-forward layer, we can control the number of active units and match memory requirements to available resources. Our experiments demonstrate that Gating Dropout not only conserves memory, but it also enhances the performance of transformers on tasks like language modeling and machine translation. Moreover, we've found that Gating Dropout can be used to model the effects of different hardware constraints, allowing us to compare the performance of various models in a more systematic way. Overall, Gating Dropout offers a practical solution for working with transformers in low-memory environments. The accompanying code and additional results are available on GitHub.

Furthermore, our approach was found to significantly outperform existing techniques in terms of privacy preservation. Finally, our approach was successfully applied to anonymize images from the real-world video dataset, the Citywide Surveillance (CWPS) dataset. This study investigates the effectiveness and reliability of differential privacy (DP) enhanced optimization techniques in comparison to traditional methods. Specifically, we examine the performance of regularization techniques on non-convex problems when combined with differential private regularization. Our analysis reveals that the performance of DP-enhanced models is heavily influenced by the specific algorithm and problem structure used. In some cases, we found that traditional regularization techniques can achieve better results than DP-enhanced methods, particularly when focusing on model accuracy rather than overall utility. Additionally, we highlight the benefits of DP-enhanced optimization, including improved robustness to data noise and better generalization performance in certain scenarios. Our results suggest that DP-enhanced models can be a valuable tool for identifying optimal hyperparameters and model structures, particularly in high-dimensional data. Finally, we discuss the trade-offs between DP-enhanced optimization and data privacy, and propose strategies for balancing these competing demands. Our findings are based on a range of experiments using popular deep learning models, including ResNet, VGG, and DenseNet. The JADE framework, a widely-used Java-based agent platform, has a significant memory footprint due to its native agent components. Our work presents a novel in-memory agent system called "Steady and Scalable JADE" (S2JADE), which is specifically designed to run within memory-constrained environments. S2JADE achieves this by leveraging a combination of in-memory agent components and a lightweight, event-driven, and time-efficient broadcast mechanism. Additionally, we have developed an in-memory agent management system called "in-memory broker", which facilitates agent scalability through the use of unique identifiers and a centralized registry. Our evaluation of S2JADE in a cloud-based environment demonstrates its potential to handle large volumes of concurrent messages with minimal latency. Specifically, we have successfully tested the platform with 100,000 agents and 10,000 concurrent messages of varying sizes, achieving an average latency of 0.2 ms and an average throughput of 50,000 messages per second. Moreover, we have also successfully integrated S2JADE with the "JADE Agentgraph" and "WebGloos" systems, enabling seamless communication between in-memory agents and the external world. Our evaluation results suggest that S2JADE outperforms JADE by a factor of 10 in terms of agent performance and a factor of 5 in terms of agent scalability. Finally, we have also explored the feasibility of utilizing S2JADE in real-time systems, and we have identified its potential applications in the context of Internet of Things. understanding and interpretation, often influencing our perception of the
underlying message. Effective communication relies on a balance between
presenting details and compressing complex data to make it more readable.

data, including text, images, and videos, to determine the optimal level of
information loss for different purposes. Our findings suggest that a
specific level of compression, which preserves 10-20% of the original details,
results in the greatest variety of visual depictions for most categories of
data. Our research has far-reaching implications for the fields of
communication, design, and multimedia production. Furthermore, our
analysis of human perception in response to compressed media reveals that
our brains adapt to these depictions and can distinguish them from original
content even when the majority of the details are lost, reaching
confidence levels of 95% or higher. Our findings also indicate that
compressing media by 50% or more can lead to significant variations in how
they are perceived, achieving a high level of statistical discrimination
between compressed and uncompressed media (p < 10^-4). These results have
important implications for the fields of media production, design, and
human perception. Our research has been made available in an open-access

the following website: https://www.3rdvision.org/compression. Additionally,
our data and analysis tools are available for use in R, and can be accessed
at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/ThreeD-VI/VISCOM.

This approach enables us to establish a connection between the computational simulations and an existing lower bound for traditional Ramsey numbers, while also allowing us to derive new upper bounds for certain hypergraph pairs. This discovery is used to establish an upper bound for the Ramsey number of a particular hypergraph and graph combination. These calculations are supported by computational evidence provided in a supplementary appendix. dependencies effectively. However, little is known about how the use of feature
toggles impacts the review and testing processes in software projects. To address

open-source Java projects, analyzing the relationship between feature toggles and
pull request characteristics. Our findings indicate that the use of feature
toggles is associated with reduced review times, comment numbers, and test-related

We introduce a novel self-supervised denoising technique called Decay2Distill, which enhances the performance of existing methods by incorporating a dual approach. Current methods primarily focus on adapting feature representations to new tasks using meta-learning, but often struggle with task drift and inadequate task representations. In today's world, social media has a profound impact on how people form their opinions and perspectives. This study aims to explore the influence of social media on belief formation, specifically focusing on the two main factors: the majority and minority opinions. We investigate how social media algorithms, which are typically designed to promote content that is popular among users, shape individuals' beliefs. We examine the effects of these algorithms, as well as alternative scenarios where only majority or minority opinions are favored. Our analysis reveals that the default setting, which favors majority opinions, can exacerbate the polarization of beliefs. In contrast, promoting minority opinions leads to a more diverse distribution of beliefs. Surprisingly, the outcome also depends on the initial state of majority opinions, with the ability to counterbalance polarization dependent on their presence or absence at the start. This study highlights the need for social media platforms to develop more thoughtful belief-forming tools, taking into account the potential consequences of their algorithms, rather than solely focusing on popular content. These tools should strive to promote the coexistence of diverse perspectives and counterbalance extreme views, in order to foster a more open-minded society. and estimate their corresponding descriptors. By integrating an attention module

faster processing. On the widely used BonoReg dataset, AA3DNet surpasses its 
competitors with an accuracy of 85.00%. Furthermore, our method exhibits 
competitive performance on the more demanding PanoContext and T-Net datasets.

We introduce a new deep neural network architecture called ParaNet, designed for processing 3D geometric data. ParaNet consists of layers of para-unit cells, which are three-dimensional extensions of the standard building blocks of convolutional neural networks. Each para-unit cell aggregates local point cloud information in three-dimensional space, and can be used to either reduce the point cloud's dimensionality or generate new feature information. Building upon this framework, we propose ParaNet, a network that uses para-unit cells to build a consistent, multi-layered representation of 3D geometric data. This consistent representation enables the development of a unified, end-to-end learning framework for a wide range of 3D tasks, including registration and segmentation. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of ParaNet in achieving state-of-the-art performance across various 3D tasks, and show that it can be optimized for different applications by adjusting the para-unit cells. Federated learning has emerged as a promising approach to training machine learning models on diverse, decentralized data sets while maintaining user privacy. Despite its benefits, current methods often favor data sets with superior quality and overlook disparities in data across different subgroups. These limitations can lead to inaccurate model predictions and exacerbate existing social inequalities. To address these issues, we introduce a framework called Fairness-aware Federated Training (FaFeT) that promotes fairness and accuracy by identifying and minimizing disparities in data quality and accuracy across different subgroups. FaFeT uses a combination of fairness and accuracy metrics to optimize the training process and produces models that are not only accurate but also fair. Our experimental results demonstrate that FaFeT outperforms other methods in achieving fairness and accuracy on datasets with diverse quality and accuracy across different subgroups. speech-to-text translation for languages and dialects with limited or no
existing training data, without using audio. This innovation employs a
conditional language model to translate languages into a hypothetical, abstract
sound representation system, making it possible to create a new ASR system for

with limited or no available training data, and achieved accurate translation on

this sound representation system. This research has the potential to greatly

The process of analyzing visual data is crucial in various fields, yet examining large amounts of information can be overwhelming and ineffective. To address this issue, we conducted a series of experiments where participants were asked to identify the shapes within images under two different conditions: with a time limit and without one. Our findings show that imposing a time constraint leads to a shift in focus during the examination, leading to more consistent and accurate identifications of shapes among inconsistent human judgments. These results support the idea that strategic information gathering is an effective way to make the most out of limited visual inspection time. To validate our findings, we also explored the potential of using an information-theoretic approach to identify the most informative areas of images and shapes, with promising results. Our research contributes to the development of strategies for efficient visual analysis and efficient resource allocation in various fields. The data collected from our study may serve as a valuable resource for evaluating the effectiveness of these strategies. This paper introduces a highly robust sparse dataset that mimics real-world patterns in the fractal sequence.  The data is generated using a simple formula, but when noise is added, it becomes challenging for traditional machine learning models to distinguish between the signal and noise, leading to poor performance.  To address this issue, we created a new dataset that retains the core signal but eliminates most of the noise, effectively testing the robustness of learning algorithms.  Our new dataset, in combination with a simple formula, enables a realistic simulation of real-world data, allowing us to evaluate the effectiveness of state-of-the-art machine learning models.  The performance difference between learning from the original noisy dataset and the new robust one is substantial, as confirmed by our experiments.  Ultimately, this study aims to provide a new benchmark for evaluating the robustness of machine learning models. An investigation into CP violation in specific B decays is conducted, specifically those that produce D0 particles that then decay into hadronic states. This analysis focuses on two distinct scenarios: one in which the hadronic states consist of two kaons, and another in which they consist of a kaon and a pion. A search for CP-violating differences in the rates of these decays under charge-concurrent and charge-concurrent conditions is performed, as well as a search for a difference in the rates of D0 decays into different states. The research finds no notable CP-violating effects and places 95% confidence upper limits on CP-violating differences in the rates of these decays. Recent studies have demonstrated that a pre-trained multilingual language model (MLM) can successfully forecast economic indicators in low-resource languages. This study examines the effectiveness of MLM in predicting economic data, revealing that its performance stems from a combination of cross-lingual representation capabilities and inherent properties of the data. We also identify limitations in MLM's ability to generalize to other domains, which are largely attributed to the limitations of the data itself rather than the model's architecture. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing MLM-based methods. Furthermore, we provide insights into the relationships between MLM's cross-lingual representation capabilities and forecasting performance. Our findings offer practical guidance for improving forecasting capabilities in low-resource languages. In a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system, we investigate the achievable rates for transmitting K independent messages over a fading channel with N transmit antennas, subject to power constraints per message. By analyzing the achievable rates in the finite blocklength regime, we identify the optimal multiple selection strategies for both multiple and random antenna selections. The study reveals that, unlike in the asymptotic regime, fully random antenna selection can outperform multiple selection strategies, a phenomenon attributed to the finite blocklength regime's distinct characteristics. The findings are further validated through simulations. To facilitate practical applications, we develop suboptimal multiple selection strategies that balance performance with reduced computational complexity. The proposed approaches are evaluated through simulations and shown to yield improved results. Specifically, we demonstrate that, in comparison to multiple selection strategies, our proposed schemes exhibit significant performance gains, amounting to up to 20% in certain scenarios. The proposed strategies are particularly beneficial in low SNR conditions and short blocklength scenarios. Ultimately, we highlight the importance of considering the finite blocklength regime in wireless communication design. The associated source code is publicly available for reference purposes. In this paper, we introduce a novel model for crystalline cohomology that employs "obtained sheaves," yielding a model that is both bornological and efficient. Notably, we demonstrate that the derived category of obtained sheaves is equivalent to the perfect derived category of rings of Tate modules, thereby resolving a previously open question of Bouzat and Kerz. Secure operating systems require robust protection from malicious software, which they achieve by enforcing strict rules on data access point in the kernel. Traditionally, the kernel's security features are implemented through intricate and custom code that handles memory exceptions in the program. However, this approach leads to vulnerabilities and inefficient performance. We introduce Fuel, a compiler-based solution that embeds memory management capabilities into the kernel to prevent common memory-related security threats in programs. By leveraging a standardized interface, Fuel allows the kernel to efficiently handle memory exceptions in a wide range of applications. We have successfully integrated Fuel into the Linux kernel and evaluated its performance on various systems, demonstrating its ability to provide reliable and efficient security without compromising system functionality. Our results show that Fuel's security features do not come at the cost of performance, with a small overhead of 1.3-4.0% in CPU usage and less than 1% increase in memory consumption. This approach enables secure software development and reliable data access, paving the way for the creation of more trustworthy systems. To mitigate these issues, alternative approaches such as edge computing and device-to-device (D2D) offloading have been explored, but they often lack user-centricity and edge device resources. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel approach called Self-Managed IoT, which enables full user control over offloading decisions by employing a two-tier offloading framework. The proposed framework allows users to select between device offloading, edge computing, and D2D offloading, while also considering the user's role in the offloading process. The experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework in optimizing performance metrics and validate its feasibility on real-world devices. To the best knowledge, this is the first study to investigate self-managed IoT offloading with a user-centric approach. The study also identifies future research directions in this area. In this paper, we address the challenge of estimating high-frequency oscillations from low-frequency data. We develop a novel estimation procedure that employs low-frequency data to construct a time-varying Fourier basis, which is then used to transform the data. The resulting time series is analyzed using a set of coefficients that represent the frequency components of interest. We propose inference procedures for these coefficients and examine their properties through theoretical and simulation-based results. The method's effectiveness is also demonstrated using high-frequency trading data. The difference between the two approaches is most pronounced in the case of analyzing high-frequency trading data. This study introduces a tethered aerial robot capable of guiding humans through physical contact towards a predetermined target. The robot's ability to control the interaction force and move towards the user's hand creates a continuous, tangible feedback loop. The key innovation lies in the development of an adaptive controller that considers the user's dynamic state, including their speed and position of contact, to achieve a smooth interaction experience. The effectiveness of this approach was evaluated through a simulation in Gazebo, revealing that the proposed controller can successfully navigate the complex dynamics of the system and achieve a stable, smooth interaction. The results also show that the controller can be seamlessly scaled up to accommodate larger systems with multiple degrees of freedom. Notably, experiments conducted in real-world settings demonstrate that the continuous feedback generated by the robot results in a pleasant, non-intrusive experience for the user, who reported a preference for this method over discrete tactile feedback. The findings of this study are intended to inform the design of haptic interfaces for various human-robot applications, including search and rescue, manufacturing, and healthcare settings. Our research delves into the effectiveness of factor models that adapt over time and those with stable factor connections in forecasting mortality within the life insurance industry. We utilize mortality data from France spanning 1968-2018 and employ various factor models, including those with time-dependent and time-stationary loadings, to make predictions about future mortality trends. The results indicate that models employing fixed loadings yield superior results compared to their time-dependent counterparts, even when allowing for unobserved components. We also compare the performance of factor models to a widely used multi-state life table approach and find that the latter outperforms factor models in predicting mortality. However, the life tables struggle to accurately forecast mortality levels more than 20 years in advance. We further investigate the resilience of our findings when faced with unobserved shocks, such as the 1980 and 1989 events, and conclude that the life tables exhibit greater sensitivity to these events compared to the factor models employed. The research is intended to provide insights for actuaries and policymakers seeking to improve mortality forecasts. Two additional appendices are provided to facilitate the practical application of our findings by offering a user-friendly implementation of the factor models and providing sample mortality data. This research introduces the PRCA dataset, a comprehensive and accurate collection of 1,500 annotated videos featuring 75 hours of intense exercise. Each video is labeled with precise heart rate measurements taken every 30 seconds through a wearable wrist device. Our study demonstrates the practicality of using PRCA for predicting heart rate during vigorous physical activity, as well as evaluating existing video-based activity recognition and machine learning techniques. We establish new standards for evaluating heart rate prediction models by comparing them to manual, medically-approved annotations. Furthermore, we propose a novel deep learning approach called Attention-based Dense Network (ADenseNet), which achieves superior performance on PRCA and surpasses or competes with leading techniques in predicting heart rates during intense exercise. ADenseNet's code and the PRCA dataset are freely accessible at https://github.com/zhongxichang/PRCA. Our dataset and results serve as a foundation for future research on predicting heart rates during vigorous physical activity. Our approach is applicable to a broad range of situations, including autonomous driving, smart homes, and industrial automation. This research provides a foundation for a more secure and robust deployment of reinforcement learning agents in real-world applications. Additionally, we've identified areas for future investigation, including the development of algorithms that can detect and counter reward manipulation attempts. Data discretization is a crucial step in the data preprocessing process, significantly enhancing machine learning model performance.  Among various techniques, discretization methods based on decision trees and random splits have gained widespread acceptance.  However, these methods often struggle to balance the importance of relevant data and its distribution, leading to suboptimal performance.  In response, this study introduces a novel max-relevance-min-divergence standard, aiming to strike a better balance between the two.  By leveraging this standard, a new discretization approach is developed, which is shown to outperform existing methods through experimental analysis of its classification accuracy on multiple datasets using naive Bayes.  The results demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits improved performance in handling datasets with varying characteristics.  Furthermore, this study provides insights into the application of the max-relevance-min-divergence standard in machine learning, highlighting its potential to address related research challenges in the future.

This paper introduces a novel continuous action reinforcement learning method, referred to as CAL, which employs a Gaussian distribution for actions. We demonstrate that CAL can be reformulated as a problem of minimizing the variance of a target function, which can be efficiently addressed using gradient descent. This transformation enables the derivation of a closed-form expression for the optimal action, facilitating the development of an efficient CAL algorithm. Our study also investigates the convergence of CAL, and provides a lower bound on the sample complexity required for CAL to achieve sub-optimal results. Furthermore, we extend the applicability of CAL to the regulation of continuous quantum systems by formulating the latter as a discrete quantum Markov decision process. This is achieved by partitioning the state space and discretizing the action space. Our proposed CAL algorithm is then adapted to address this discrete quantum MDP. Finally, we validate the efficacy of CAL through numerical simulations of a quantum system subject to disturbance. These simulations demonstrate that CAL can effectively stabilize the quantum system. This research paper investigates $n$-generator algebras formed over associative rings. We derive an upper limit for $n$ in relation to the ring and its free algebra. We establish specific conditions that result in free algebras of three generator types and characterize certain classes of rings using universal coalgebraic frameworks. These findings also apply to group and groupoid algebras in analogous ways. We provide an illustrative counterexample to show that three-generator types are possible in group algebras even with relatively simple group structures. Additionally, our work demonstrates that the number of three-generator types for group algebras is not determined solely by the group's Abelianizability. We also discuss potential generalizations of our results to other types of algebras and present relevant open problems for future investigation. Lastly, we provide an appendix outlining some foundational universal coalgebraic results for the benefit of readers unfamiliar with these concepts. This study introduces the uneven Tobit examination as a novel method for measuring correlations in data sets affected by censoring. The uneven Tobit examination surpasses existing approaches in two key aspects: it enables users to detect even the slightest correlations (down to a certain threshold) and it provides users with the flexibility to specify different correlation assumptions for various groups within their data set. The uneven Tobit examination achieves this through the application of the uneven Tobit model, a two-part model that accounts for the unequal distribution of variables. The model's first part models the presence of non-zero values, and the second part models the distribution of non-zero values. We propose a novel estimation method that leverages the asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators to obtain correlation estimates. This method is compared to existing correlation assessment methods, such as Spearman and Kendall rank correlation coefficients and the Tobit examination, using both simulated data sets and real-world examples. The results demonstrate that the uneven Tobit examination offers improved accuracy in correlation assessment, particularly in cases where correlations are weak. Furthermore, our method is computationally efficient and can be easily implemented in practical settings. The proposed approach is expected to be a valuable tool for researchers seeking to detect correlations in data sets with censoring. For instance, it can be applied to medical studies where certain patient data may be incomplete or subject to censoring, such as in studies of chronic diseases. The proposed method can also be used in social sciences, such as social network analysis, to detect correlations in data sets with different network structures. Notably, our algorithm circumvents the need for full model space diagonalization, allowing for more streamlined processing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm by applying it to the two-site Fermi-Hubbard model, where the spatially localized nature of the physical operators facilitates efficient implementation. Furthermore, our algorithm's performance is evaluated using a quantum device that simulates the dynamics of a two-site Fermi-Hubbard model. By comparing the results from our algorithm with those from full model space diagonalization, we confirm the algorithm's ability to accurately capture the system's behavior. This algorithm's capabilities are also showcased through the simulation of a three-site Fermi-Hubbard model on a quantum device. Overall, our results indicate that this algorithm holds promise for the efficient simulation of complex quantum systems, particularly those exhibiting multiple regions of interaction. By converting Go source code into an abstract syntax tree and then evaluating it, BinGo is capable of detecting a range of concurrency flaws, including those related to goroutine synchronization, channel data access, goroutine leaks, resource leaks, and mismatched goroutine closures. On average, it took 12.5 seconds to complete the analysis of 1,000 Java programs, whereas it took 44.6 seconds to complete the analysis of 1,000 Go programs. Furthermore, our study found that Go programs contain a higher incidence of concurrency flaws, with 1,000 Go programs exhibiting 2.5 flaws on average, compared to 0.4 in Java. Our research also reveals that Go programs tend to have more complex flaws, with a higher average number of fault-prone statements at 12.3 for Go and 5.0 for Java. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of BinGo in detecting a wide variety of concurrency flaws in Go programs. Our research also highlights the need for further investigation into the impact of concurrency control on Go program analysis. Recent advancements in self-supervised learning have led to significant breakthroughs in pre-training visual representations, particularly through image generation and object detection tasks. Nonetheless, the majority of research in this area has focused on predicting a single possible future outcome for a given image, neglecting the multiple potential futures an object can encounter. This paper seeks to address this limitation by introducing the Multi-future Pathway Prediction (MPP) task, which involves generating a diverse set of future image variations from a single input image. This task is achieved by tracing the trajectories of objects over time and leveraging the inherent diversity of object motion. The MPP task is then integrated with existing pre-trained image generation and object detection models to showcase their capabilities. The results demonstrate that models can effectively generate a wide range of future images, highlighting the value of exploring multiple potential futures for visual representation learning. This research aims to stimulate further investigation into learning object dynamics and advancing pre-trained image and object representation models. An optimal consensus algorithm is derived to minimize the sum of squared errors within the network, and its effectiveness is demonstrated using a numerical simulation. Conversational AI agents must possess certain essential qualities in order to effectively interact with human users as part of a human-computer dialogue system. This paper examines the importance of these characteristics from both theoretical and practical perspectives. We propose that these necessary qualities can be broadly classified into two key areas: persona and knowledge. We propose a new persona representation framework that incorporates the concept of a persona-knowledge network, which enables the creation of tailored dialogue systems by combining persona and knowledge attributes in a flexible manner. This approach allows for the generation of diverse conversational responses while maintaining consistency within a persona's overall style. We also introduce a persona-knowledge network that utilizes a graph neural network to model both persona and knowledge attributes in a unified manner. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in generating more natural-sounding and informative conversations compared to existing approaches, while also providing additional analysis to support our claims. Our research aims to facilitate the development of more sophisticated and versatile conversational AI systems. The ultimate goal of model checkpoints is to facilitate rapid knowledge transfer between models, yet current methods for utilizing them for transfer learning are limited. This paper delves into the fundamental challenge of knowledge transfer from pre-trained models, revealing that the traditional approach of directly updating the model's parameters can be inefficient. By examining the dynamics of gradient flow, we discovered that fine-tuning a model with a limited number of epochs may overlook the contributions of earlier layers, hindering the model's ability to retain knowledge. To overcome this limitation, we developed a novel technique, called Fine-Tune-Refine, which selectively updates the model's parameters to retain previously acquired knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate that Fine-Tune-Refine consistently outperforms fine-tuning alone, achieving higher accuracy on critical benchmarks such as ImageNet and ResNet variants. Our work paves the way for future research into effective checkpoint usage, enabling more efficient and high-accuracy model development. Deep learning models often rely on convolutional kernels as their basic building blocks, but their performance is limited by the availability of training data and the need for pre-defined kernel specifications. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a novel approach called MetaKernel, which enables the training of convolutional networks with randomly generated kernels, and the acquisition of new kernels from a set of labeled examples. By leveraging a variational inference framework, MetaKernel can automatically select the most informative features from a large pool of examples and produce a corresponding set of random kernels, leading to improved model performance and generalizability. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of MetaKernel through experiments on various classification tasks, including those with limited labeled data and samples, and shown that it outperforms traditional kernels in terms of accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, MetaKernel can produce multiple kernel versions from a single set of labeled examples, and these kernels can be used to train independent networks, leading to improved model diversity and generalizability. Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) remains a leading method for approximating expectations of smooth functions with respect to Gaussian distributions. However, its performance may significantly deteriorate for non-convex functions due to the curse of dimensionality. This research investigates whether LMC can be improved for non-convex functions by identifying a broader class of functions with positive curvature that are bounded below. We introduce a new concept of non-log-concave sampling and develop a general framework for analyzing non-log-convex functions. We then show that LMC can be improved for non-log-concave sampling by providing a new first-order stationarity bound that holds for any step-size and finite number of samples. This result is further demonstrated through numerical experiments, indicating that our new approach can substantially reduce the number of samples required for a given level of accuracy. Moreover, our approach can be easily extended to the more general setting of stochastic gradient Langevin Monte Carlo (SGLMC). The implications of our work are significant, as it suggests that non-convex functions may not be the main reason for the curse of dimensionality in LMC. Instead, it may be the log-concavity of functions, as our results indicate that even log-convex functions can be challenging to sample. Our research opens up new avenues of investigation, such as the design of new sampling distributions and algorithms for non-log-concave sampling. These topics are left for future study. A significant challenge in simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) involves accurately determining the relative positions and orientations of different landmarks. This research addresses the issue of localized rotation, where a camera's reference point is fixed within a known environment. To achieve this, we develop a novel approach called the viewing graph, which represents the relationships between distinct camera viewpoints. Our contribution is the Resolving Viewing Graph enhancement method, which refines this graph to ensure accurate relative positions and orientations are calculated. This approach involves two key components: a graph resolution process that prioritizes and recalculates the relationships between different viewpoints, and a rotation refinement process that incorporates this enhanced graph. Through simulations and real-world implementation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately determining camera poses and rotations. Furthermore, we show that our method significantly outperforms existing solutions in both simulation and real-world testing. overcome them.  We begin by examining the challenges associated with Safety

practical application of our approach, we create a simulated environment and
test it using a widely used benchmark dataset.  The results show that our
method can significantly enhance the performance of Safety Overalls and

Safety Overalls.  We also provide recommendations for future research directions
in this field.  The accompanying code and dataset are available for public

MPLS networks, widely used for high-speed internet connections and high-value data transmission, pose a significant challenge for network security professionals. Current methods for detecting MPLS-based attacks fall short, requiring manual inspection that can't keep pace with rapidly evolving threat landscapes. This research introduces TNT, a system that automatically identifies and tracks MPLS tunnels in real-time, enabling the analysis of attack vectors and the detection of potential threats. Through large-scale experiments, we've found that TNT accurately detects more than 99% of incoming MPLS packets, marking it as the first practical system for this complex task. Additionally, TNT allows network operators to identify and mitigate threats with minimal administrative effort, providing a crucial step towards protecting the integrity of networks like those operated by Internet Exchange Point (IXP) operators. A novel approach to motion planning known as Instantaneous Pathway Smoothing with Neural Networks (IPSNN) has been developed, which uses neural networks to generate smooth and collision-free paths. Unlike traditional sampling-based methods, IPSNN uses real-time trajectory optimization to improve upon previously calculated paths. By leveraging neural networks to handle optimization sub-problems, IPSNN achieves faster computation times and more accurate results, which can be further improved by incorporating additional data. A comparative study found that IPSNN outperforms other methods in terms of both computation time and quality of motion plans. Moreover, IPSNN can be easily adapted to suit different planning objectives and can handle a variety of scenarios, including those with moving obstacles, which makes it a versatile and efficient tool for real-time motion planning tasks. A source code implementation of IPSNN is available for public use. The challenge of assessing the state of a distant entity is a critical issue in
quantum communication systems, particularly when intercepting states can compromise
privacy. We investigate strategies for assessing the state of a sender while
preventing an eavesdropper from doing so. Building on a previous approach, we
introduce a new method that uses a specific type of measurement to achieve this
goal. This approach is then tested in various scenarios, including quantum key
distribution protocols, to assess its effectiveness. Our findings demonstrate
that this method can effectively protect against eavesdropping in certain
circumstances, but may not always be suitable for practical applications. We
conclude that a single assessment method cannot effectively safeguard against
all potential threats to security in quantum communication systems. Instead, a
comprehensive security solution may require the combination of multiple
approaches tailored to specific use cases. Additional research is needed to
fully realize the potential of quantum communication systems in this regard. The

Recent research has highlighted the importance of balancing robustness against adversarial attacks and achieving high accuracy in deep neural network learning to ensure reliable real-world performance. This concept is particularly relevant in robotics, where critical safety functions require models that can effectively generalize and perform in diverse, unpredictable environments. This study investigates the relationship between these two key learning objectives in robotics through comprehensive experiments on a range of tasks, including visual perception and control. Our findings indicate that current techniques used to enhance robustness do not consistently improve accuracy and may even degrade it in some cases. Furthermore, we found that adversarial attacks are highly effective in disrupting robotic behavior, with 80% of attacks resulting in errors on safety-critical parameters. These results suggest that traditional metrics used to gauge robustness in computer vision may not be applicable to robotics and that a more comprehensive approach is needed to evaluate the robustness of robotic models. To address this challenge, we propose a new evaluation metric that takes into account the spatial distribution of errors and their impact on robotic behavior. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective in improving the robustness of robotic models without compromising their accuracy. This research contributes to the development of more reliable robotic systems by highlighting the importance of balancing robustness and accuracy and providing a new framework for evaluating the robustness of robotic models. The code and datasets used in this study will be made available publicly. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between robustness and accuracy in deep learning, with a focus on its relevance to robotic systems. The integration of machine learning algorithms in the geoscience field has been rapidly adopted, particularly in the analysis of seismic data, due to their ability to simplify complex tasks. However, implementing these algorithms in a way that allows geoscine researchers to understand their inner workings is crucial. This research proposes a novel approach that combines a Collaborative Inversion-Segmentation method with a human-centered collaborative framework. This method enables geoscience experts to leverage machine learning tools, such as neural networks, without losing their interpretability. By applying a neural network to invert seismic data, a segmentation map is generated that highlights the structure of the subsurface. This segmentation map is then used to create a geological interpretation, which is further refined by the human expert. This refinement process is then fed back into the neural network, allowing it to generate a more accurate interpretation. This process can be repeated, creating a feedback loop between the neural network and human expert. This collaborative approach has been tested on a real-world dataset and has shown promising results. The paper concludes by discussing potential future applications of this method. This research was presented at the 2021 EAGE Conference & Exhibition and was published in the conference's proceedings. The full research paper is available online. Temporal patterns within high-dimensional biological data, such as gene expression, present a challenge for understanding biological processes. To uncover these hidden patterns, we develop a new approach combining factor analysis and vector autoregressions to segment time series data. By integrating prior knowledge, we use group vector autoregressions to estimate temporal relationships and factor models to capture common trends. A Bayesian nonnegative least squares algorithm is employed for inference, and we apply our method to simulated data, single-cell RNA sequencing, and human transcriptional profiles, demonstrating its effectiveness in uncovering meaningful clusters of genes and responding groups. Our method outperforms existing techniques, such as dynamic mode decomposition of extreme events, and provides a unique perspective on gene expression, revealing distinct patterns of gene activity. By applying our method to single-cell RNA sequencing, we identify significant changes in gene expression across developmental stages and cellular states. Furthermore, we successfully uncover gene patterns associated with human diseases, revealing novel insights into the progression of multiple sclerosis. Our method also detects gene patterns associated with the progression of breast cancer, revealing genes that may be involved in the disease's progression. Overall, our method provides a powerful tool for uncovering hidden patterns in high-dimensional temporal data, revealing new insights into the complex dynamics of biological processes. By incorporating a unique constraint that preserves occlusion patterns in the views, the OEC method effectively reduces occlusion artifacts. The OEC method has been successfully integrated into a two-stage optimization framework, which first estimates depth and occlusion maps from images using a coarse-to-fine approach.
